text: Microsoft’s backing for the data centre in Loughton, Essex, formed part of its pledge to invest £22bn in the UK Credit : tupungato James Titcomb Technology Editor Show biography James Titcomb is The Telegraph's Technology Editor and has covered the tech industry for a decade from Silicon Valley and London. He can be reached at james.titcomb@telegraph.co.uk and on X at @jamestitcomb Microsoft has pulled out of an Essex data centre deal in a blow to British company Nscale’s plans for a multibillion-dollar listing. The US tech giant, one of Nscale’s two largest customers, recently informed the company that it was pulling the plug on its agreement, which was announced last year. It is a significant setback for Nscale, given Microsoft was to become the anchor tenant at the company’s first British data centre in Loughton, Essex . Microsoft’s decision threatens to undermine Nscale’s attempts to push ahead with a Wall Street flotation worth up to $35bn (£26bn), despite a brutal sell-off in AI computing stocks. Rival data centre developers have seen their share prices plunge over the last week on concerns that they will struggle to repay their debts as interest rates and inflation continue to rise. The outcome of Nscale’s attempted stock market listing will be viewed as a crucial litmus test of investors’ continued appetite for debt-hungry AI businesses. Its success or otherwise will also have implications for Britain’s broader aspirations for the technology. Nscale, which is backed by tech giants including Nvidia, has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” data centre provider. Microsoft was expected to become the anchor tenant at Nscale’s data centre in Loughton, Essex Ministers have talked up its Essex data centre project as emblematic of the UK’s AI ambitions, and have lobbied local councillors to push it through. Microsoft’s backing for the project formed part of £22bn in UK investments promised by the tech company last year during Donald Trump’s state visit. Sir Keir Starmer said it was a step towards Britain “becoming a world leader in AI” . The data centre site, which contains thousands of high-end Nvidia AI chips, was originally intended to come online next year. However, it has faced repeated delays, with grid bosses telling Nscale that they do not expect a power supply until the 2030s. Microsoft’s cancellation leaves the site in apparent limbo. The company was its only announced customer, having agreed to rent 23,000 Nvidia AI chips at the facility. Financing for the data centre boom hinges on securing long-term commitments from AI giants to buy up capacity. More than 40pc of Nscale’s $103bn in contracted revenue comes from Microsoft, although the UK deal is believed to be a small part of that. Anthropic is another major customer. Nscale, which boasts heavyweights including former Facebook executives Sheryl Sandberg and Sir Nick Clegg on its board, has been privately valued at $15bn. It is seeking to raise billions of dollars in a float that could value it at more than twice that, making it one of Britain’s most valuable AI companies. However, its plans have clashed with a major sell-off in AI infrastructure businesses amid questions about the data centre building boom. Tech analyst Gartner said last week that $3.5tn could be written off by 2030 if the AI boom fails to deliver on its promises. Separately, Nscale has also faced delays at a flagship data centre in Norway, reportedly leading to heavy penalties. Australian rival Firmus cancelled plans for a $20bn IPO earlier this month, citing market conditions. Other “neocloud” companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius have seen their shares and bonds slump. Neoclouds are heavily dependent on raising new investment and debt to keep building, and soaring market interest rates have increased concerns about the sustainability of their business models. An Nscale spokesman said: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK. “Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.” Microsoft did not comment. Nscale was founded by Australian entrepreneur Josh Payne, a former coal miner, just two years ago, and has faced scrutiny for signing large contracts despite a lack of a track record in building data centres. However, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, praised Nscale on Wednesday at an event in London, saying: “You could be the most valuable UK startup they have created in the last 10 years.” High electricity prices and long waits for grid connections have been seen as a major barrier to building AI infrastructure in Britain. In April, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI suspended plans for a “ Stargate” AI facility with Nscale on Tyneside, citing Britain’s high electricity prices.
